To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
mild stroke leads to no changes in multi-fingers synergies, but to a delay in anticipatory adjustments of the synergic control.

1) the stroke patients showed lower maximum force production in the contralesion hand; 2) the patients showed increased inter-finger enslaving; 3) the patients showed delayed feedforward adjustments of multi-finger synergistic control; 4) there were no significant changes in the multi-finger synergy index during steady-state production.
the patients with history of unilateral stroke showed lower maximal finger force production, in particular in their contralesional hand.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of synergies in the control of human multi-joint movements and their impairment in stroke.
the role of multi-finger synergic control during force production.
the effects of unilateral stroke on the control of multi-finger synergic force production.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the stroke patients showed a significant reduction in the maximal finger forces in both hands, increased finger enslaving in the contralesion hand, and a delay in the anticipatory feed-forward synergy adjustments prior to quick actions.
stroke affects feed-forward control of synergies, enslaving and maximal force production.
the feed-forward control of synergies is impaired in stroke patients.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
cortical stroke leads to impairment in the feed-forward control of synergies and enslaving, but not to the steady-state synergies.
cortical stroke affects feedforward synergistic adjustments, but not the steady state synergistic control.
stroke patients with mild deficits have a reduced ability to adjust multi-finger synergic control prior to a quick movement and an increase in the interdependence among the fingers.
The main takeaway from our work is that
stroke affects the feed-forward control of synergies prior to an action, but not their on-line control.
the feed-forward control of the multi-finger synergic control is more sensitive to stroke than the feed-back control.
the feed-forward adjustments of multi-finger synergistic control may be more vulnerable to stroke than the synergies themselves.
